To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cadmium levels in corn grain from sludge‐treated fields were within acceptable limits and that the cadmium concentration in stover from the sludge‐treatment fields was elevated above that of stover from non‐sludge‐treated plots, but the levels were not phytotoxic.
the disposal of digested sludge on crop producing land may not be hazardous to human and animal heath if the plant material does not contain elevated levels of some toxic heavy metals.

(1) cadmium concentration in grain was not affected by sludge application; (2) cadmium concentration was elevated in stover from treated plots but was below toxic levels; and (3) the cadmium content of stover decreased over the three years of sludge application.

the cadmium concentration and distribution in plants grown on a calcereous soil for three year after three annual sludges applications.
the effects of three annual applications of sewage sludge on the cadmium concentration in the grain and stover of corn (Zea may L.) grown on calcareous soil.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cadmium concentration in the corn grain from sludge‐treated plots did not exceed the 1 ppm limit recommended by the US Food and Drug Administration.
the disposal of digested sludge on land does not appear to be a hazard to human health.
the disposal of sludge on agricultural land does not pose a hazard to the food chain if the sludge contains less than 5 ppm cadmium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cadmium is not a phytotoxic metal in corn grown on calcareous soils and that the cadmium in the stover is of no concern.
cadmium levels in corn stover were elevated, but not to toxic levels, after sludge applications ceased.
sludge application did not result in elevated cadmium concentrations in corn grain but did result in elevated concentrations in corn stover.

the disposal of sludge on land does not appear to pose an environmental risk for the cadmium content of corn grain and stovers, but may pose a risk for other metals such as lead and zinc.
